analysis:
Examined the docs change in docs/provider/troubleshooting.md (head lines 83 and 143), which adds the `coordinator traffic` doctor check and describes the idle-only re-registration of unauthorized connections. I also examined the new UnauthorizedConnectionRecovery.swift (head lines 13-49). Documentation drift here does not change security controls.

UnauthorizedConnectionRecovery is a pure scheduling and predicate helper. It issues no authorization itself and makes no trust decision. shouldReconnect (lines 23-31) requires a non-nil unauthorizedSince, !busy, and elapsed >= 15 min plus per-process jitter. Retries back off from 30 min, doubling to a 4 h cap (lines 33-36). A re-registration starts a fresh coordinator verification session, so it cannot grant serving permission; the coordinator remains the sole authority over App Attest grants (A-016, T-052, T-053, TB-011). A malicious provider can already reconnect at will, so provider-driven re-registration adds no capability and is bounded against fleet load.

connectionLacksAuthorization (lines 42-49) is driven by self-reported daemon state and only gates reconnection. It treats `authorization.path == "legacy"` as not lacking authorization and a missing authorization object as not judged. A wrong result can only trigger or suppress a reconnect and never changes routing.

Limits: unit 47f42b08690f9b5f:0 (ServingReadiness.swift, 174 lines) was supplied as metadata only, with no text. Only a truncated patch excerpt was visible, so I could not review it. The call sites (ProviderLoop+ServingAuthorizationRecovery.swift) and the `busy` computation (whether accepted requests, loads and drain are all covered), plus the DaemonState.Trust and authorization.hasCurrentAppAttestAuthorization semantics, were not supplied. Integration should confirm that a reconnect cannot interrupt in-flight consumer requests (A-001 availability) and that ServingReadiness diagnostics do not leak identifiers into reports (T-058).
